claims.text: Rapid melt-spinning produces Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 in an as-quenched amorphous state.
The proposed intervention is annealing the as-quenched alloy at approximately 0.9·Tg for 5 minutes, followed by controlled cooling under an inert atmosphere.
Annealing at 0.9·Tg for 5 minutes will promote structural relaxation in this alloy.
The structural relaxation will reduce free volume in the amorphous matrix.
The structural relaxation will optimize short-range order in the amorphous matrix.
Sub-Tg annealing will release internal stresses through atomic rearrangements.
The specified annealing treatment permits relaxation without entering the crystallization regime.
The relaxed state will increase the kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangements that cause crystallite nucleation.
Reduced nucleation probability after annealing will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability.
The annealing treatment will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to the as-quenched condition.
Annealed samples will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than as-quenched controls.
Annealed samples will exhibit fewer crystalline phases than as-quenched controls during thermal analysis.
Applying the treatment immediately after quenching under an inert atmosphere is necessary for its effectiveness.
Significant deviations from the specified annealing temperature or duration may produce insufficient relaxation or incipient crystallization.
The safe and effective annealing window may change with alloy composition or cooling history.

contradictions.description: The intervention occurs only after quenching has already produced the amorphous state, yet it is claimed to improve glass-forming ability by lowering nucleation during formation. A post-formation treatment can test subsequent amorphous-state stability, but it cannot retroactively alter whether the preceding quench formed glass.

The hypothesis predicts improvement in both glass-forming ability and thermal stability, but the predicted outcomes and falsification experiment measure only post-quench thermal stability and crystallinity. No glass-forming-ability metric, such as critical cooling rate or critical casting thickness, is included.
